title: Word order 2: adverbs with the verb
subtitle: Emily always drives / we were also hungry / I can never remember
summary: Put adverbs like always, also and probably in the right place: before a one-word verb, after am/is/are/was/were, and after the first part of a two-word verb.

lesson.heading: Adverbs in the middle of a sentence
lesson.text: Some adverbs (for example **always, also, probably**) go with the verb in the middle of a sentence, not at the beginning or the end.

examples.text: We were feeling very tired and we **were also** hungry.

lesson.heading: One-word verbs and the verb be

left.label: Before a one-word verb (drives, cooked etc.)
left.text: If the verb is one word, the adverb goes before it. These adverbs also go before **have to**.
examples: I **almost fell** as I was going down the stairs.
I cleaned the house and **also cooked** the dinner. (not cooked also)
Laura **hardly ever watches** television and **rarely reads** newspapers.
'Shall I give you my address?' 'No, I **already have** it.'
Joe never phones me. I **always have to** phone him. (not I have always to phone)

right.label: After am/is/are/was/were
right.text: But adverbs go after the verb **be**.
examples: We were feeling very tired and we **were also** hungry. (not also were)
You**'re always** late. You**'re never** on time.
The traffic **isn't usually** as bad as it was this morning.

lesson.heading: Two or more verbs: adverb after the first verb
lesson.note: If the verb is two or more words (can remember, will be cancelled), the adverb usually goes after the first verb (can / doesn't / will etc.).

lesson.heading: More examples with two-word verbs
lesson.text: The same rule works with the present perfect, with can't and with questions. Note that **probably** goes before a negative (isn't / won't etc.).

examples.text: You**'ve always been** very kind to me.
Jack can't cook. He **can't even boil** an egg.
**Do** you **still work** for the same company?
The house **was only built** a year ago and it**'s already falling** down.
I **probably won't** see you. or I**'ll probably not** see you.

lesson.heading: all and both
lesson.text: We also use **all** and **both** with the verb in the middle of a sentence. They follow the same rules as the adverbs above.

examples.text: We **all felt** ill after the meal.
Sarah and Jane **have both applied** for the job.
My friends **are all going** out tonight.

lesson.heading: Short forms with is / will / did
lesson.text: Sometimes we use **is / will / did** etc. instead of repeating part of a sentence. When we do this, we put **always / never** etc. before the verb.

examples.text: Tom says he isn't clever, but I think he **is**.
He always says he won't be late, but he **always is**.
I've never done it and I **never will**.

lesson.text: Quick rule: one verb - adverb before it (she always drives); am/is/are/was/were - adverb after it (she is always late); two verbs - adverb between them (she can always drive).

exercises.explanation: With a one-word verb (drives), the adverb goes before the verb: Helen always drives to work.

exercises.statement: I'm usually hungry when I get home from work.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Adverbs go after am/is/are: I'm usually hungry.

exercises.statement: I have usually a shower in the morning.
exercises.explanation: I usually have a shower in the morning. With a one-word verb (have), the adverb goes before it.

exercises.statement: You don't listen! I have always to repeat things.
exercises.explanation: I always have to repeat things. Adverbs like always go before have to.
Adverbs go after am/is/are: Katherine is always very generous.

exercises.prompt: Martin is learning Spanish and he ___ Japanese.
exercises.explanation: With two verbs (is learning), the adverb goes after the first one: he is also learning Japanese.
The adverb goes after the first verb (don't): I don't usually have to work on Sundays.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
exercises.answer: Mark and Amy were both born in Manchester.
exercises.explanation: Both goes after the first verb (were): were both born.

exercises.prompt: How do you go to work? Ask if your friend goes by bus.
exercises.answer: Do you usually go by bus?
exercises.explanation: In a question the adverb goes after the first verb (do) and the subject: Do you usually go?

exercises.prompt: Where does the adverb go in each sentence? Sort the sentences by the rule they follow.
categories: After the first verb of two

items.text: I can never remember her name.
Do you still work for the same company?
I always have to phone him.
The meeting will probably be cancelled.

exercises.prompt: Thanks for the invitation, but ___ able to come to the party.
exercises.explanation: Probably goes before a negative: I probably won't be able to come (not I won't probably be).

exercises.prompt: Match each sentence with the sentence that follows it.

pairs.right: You always have to wait a long time to be served.
We're still living in the same place.
She can also sing very well.

pairs.left: This could be the last time I see you.

exercises.prompt: Tanya ___ that she'll phone me, but ___.
exercises.explanation: Always goes before the one-word verb (always says), and when we use does instead of repeating the verb, never goes before it (she never does).
